o: We must count pairs (i, j) with i < j and nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]. In example 1 ([1,3,2,3,1]), the pairs (1,4) and (3,4) satisfy 3 > 2*1, giving answer 2. In example 2 ([2,4,3,5,1]), the value 1 at the end forms reverse pairs with 4, 3, and 5, giving 3. A brute force double loop is O(n^2) = 2.5 * 10^9 operations for n = 5*10^4 — too slow. The key difficulty is the factor of 2 combined with values up to 2^31 in magnitude, so comparisons like nums[i] > 2*nums[j] can overflow 32-bit integers; we need an O(n log n) counting structure such as merge sort or a Fenwick tree over compressed values.
k: The condition nums[i] > 2*nums[j] only needs to be counted against elements to the left of j, so any 'count smaller/greater before me' technique applies.
Merge sort counts cross-pairs in O(n) per level while sorting, giving O(n log n) total.
Use long/64-bit arithmetic: 2 * nums[j] can exceed the 32-bit range even though nums[i] fits.

a.i: Directly check every pair (i, j) with i < j and count those where nums[i] > 2*nums[j]. This is the most literal translation of the definition and works within small limits, but at n = 5*10^4 it performs ~1.25 billion comparisons and will time out on LeetCode. It serves as a correctness baseline for testing optimized solutions.
s: For each i from 0 to n-1, for each j from i+1 to n-1:
a.t: O(n^2) — all pairs are examined once.
a.sp: O(1) — only a counter is used.

a.i: During a standard merge sort, when merging two sorted halves, every element in the right half has a larger index than every element in the left half. Because both halves are sorted, for each element y in the right half we can advance a pointer over the left half to count how many x satisfy x > 2*y — this pointer only moves forward, so counting is linear per merge. The total work is that of merge sort plus this extra linear scan.
s: Recursively split the array in half and sort each half, accumulating counts from both halves.
Before merging, use two pointers: for each y in the right half, advance pointer i while left[i] <= 2*y; add i to the count.
Merge the two sorted halves as in normal merge sort.
Return total count across all levels of recursion.
a.t: O(n log n) — log n recursion levels, each doing O(n) counting plus O(n) merging.
a.sp: O(n) — temporary buffers for merging (plus O(log n) recursion stack).

a.n: Approach 3: Binary Indexed Tree with Coordinate Compression
a.i: Process the array from right to left; for each element nums[i], we need the number of already-seen (right-side) values v with v < nums[i]/2, i.e., v such that 2*v < nums[i]. Compress all values and their halves into a sorted list of candidates, then use a Fenwick tree to query how many inserted values fall below a threshold and insert each value after querying. Each operation is O(log n).
s: Build a sorted list of all candidate values: every nums[j] and floor((nums[i]-1)/2) style thresholds (use exact halves via bisect on 2*v comparisons).
Iterate i from n-1 down to 0.
Query the BIT for the count of inserted values v with 2*v < nums[i]; add it to the answer.
Insert rank of nums[i] into the BIT.
a.t: O(n log n) — coordinate compression sorts once, then n BIT updates/queries each cost O(log n); the binary search for the threshold adds another O(log n) per element.
a.sp: O(n) — the compressed value array and Fenwick tree.

w: In an interview, lead with the merge-sort solution: it is the canonical answer, easy to explain, and reuses the classic 'count inversions' pattern with the twist of comparing against 2*y. Mention the BIT approach as an alternative if asked about online processing or other order statistics. Common pitfalls: (1) integer overflow when computing 2*nums[j] with 32-bit types — always cast to 64-bit; (2) forgetting that equal elements do not form reverse pairs (strict inequality); (3) off-by-one errors in the two-pointer scan during merge. Edge cases include single-element arrays (answer 0), all-equal arrays, large negative values, and INT_MIN where doubling overflows. Likely follow-ups: 'Count of Smaller Numbers After Self' (LC 315), 'Count Inversions', or adapting the solution to a stream of queries.
